# Requirements and their evidence, in plain English

A companion to `docs/traceability_matrix.md`. The matrix says which artifacts name a criterion; this says, for the requirements the paper's claims rest on, what the requirement asks, what does it, what the formal statements actually say, and whether that is as much as the requirement asks.

How to read it:

- The sentences are written by hand from the text of the cited statements. The identifiers, criteria, files, line numbers, statement names, tools and Evidence_Items are generated from the same data as the matrix.
- Every cited statement's text is hashed. A statement that has changed since its row was written is marked **CHANGED** below and fails `cargo xtask reqdoc --check` and the verification job, until the row is read again against the new text.
- "Proven" means a tool checked the statement against the code or the model it names. It does not mean the statement says what the requirement says: that is the fifth column.
- Evidence_Item verdicts are those of the store `target/xtask-verify/evidence` when this file was generated; an item not in that store is listed without a verdict.

- 22 of the 61 requirements have a row written by hand. The other 39 have a row generated from the requirement's own user story and the matrix, marked **not yet read**: it lists what exists and judges nothing.

| **R7** SRP dispatching (R7.1 to R7.8, Phase P1).<br>The Kernel starts a released Job only when its Priority is above both the system ceiling and every Job in progress, always picks the highest-Priority such Job (lowest Task number on a tie), and when a Job ends resumes the one it preempted, last in, first out. | Each Task has its own interrupt vector whose hardware priority is its Task Priority; the Kernel pends a vector when its Task's Job may start and sets the processor's priority mask (BASEPRI) from the ceiling, so the interrupt controller itself does the selection (crates/rsk-kernel/src/arch/cm4/entry.rs, `apply_core`). The rule the controller must realise is `Sched::eligible` and `Sched::select` in crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/sched.rs; the model of the controller is crates/rsk-logic/src/hw_model.rs.<br>Statements in: `crates/rsk-logic/src/hw_model.rs`, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/sched.rs`.<br>22 source files cite a criterion of R7 in the matrix (2 of the files above among them). | `eligible` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/sched.rs:130`): A Task is eligible when its Release is pending, it has no Job in progress, its Priority is above the system ceiling, and either no Job is in progress or its Priority is above that of the Job on top.<br>`srp_selection` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/hw_model.rs:300`): Task t is the selection when it is eligible, no Task with a pending Release has a higher Priority, and among pending Tasks of the same Priority t has the lowest index.<br>`lemma_dispatch_selects_srp_choice` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/hw_model.rs:364`): In a valid scheduler state, with the vectors mapped as the configuration says, no stale dispatch vector pending and the selected Task's vector pending, the model of the interrupt controller takes exactly that Task's vector at the present execution priority. | **Proven:** Verus (3) of the statements in column 3.<br>**Tested (QEMU):** `test-qemu-spike-p1-demo` (the demo's preemption order).<br>**Tested (rig):** `hil-dt-hw-05` (the controller takes exactly the vector above the executing level and the ceiling).<br>**Inspected:** `A4` (no stale pending dispatch vector).<br>Allocation rows: P-04, P-10.<br>Evidence_Items naming a criterion of R7: `proof-kernel-verus` (pass). | **Weaker.** R7.1 to R7.3 are proven as a statement about a model of the interrupt controller: given the Kernel's state, vectors mapped as generated, no stale pending vector and the selected Task's vector pending, the controller takes that vector and no other. The definition of 'eligible' matches R7.1 word for word (pending Release, no Job in progress, Priority above the ceiling and above the Job on top). Weaker: the tie-break is 'lowest Task index', which is one fixed order and meets R7.3 only because the design records it as the chosen order; R7.4 (what may preempt), the register state of R7.5 and the timing of R7.8 are not in these statements (registers are restored by assembly, timing is measured); and 'no stale pending vector' is a premise the entry code is trusted to establish.<br>Closed since: 2026-11-06: a dispatch vector taken inside another handler's return window raised a UsageFault on the board; a fence and a deferral close the two windows (Verification_Plan 5.8a). 2026-11-13: the assembly stubs' instruction sequences are proven against a machine model. | That the processor's interrupt controller behaves as the model (HW-01 to HW-05, HW-14) is by citation and differential tests. The stale-vector premise (A4) and that BASEPRI is written from the state after every transition are properties of the entry code, proven for the value and inspected for the write. Δ_dispatch, Δ_wake and Δ_complete are measured. |
| **R8** Resource locking and the ceiling protocol (R8.1 to R8.10, Phase P1).<br>A Job enters a shared Resource by raising the system ceiling to the Resource's ceiling and leaves by restoring it; no two Jobs are ever inside the same Resource, a Job never waits at a lock, a Job is blocked at most once per Release for at most one critical section, and no deadlock is possible. | `Sched::lock` and `unlock` keep a stack of held Resources and the ceiling (crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/sched.rs), reached through two supervisor calls; the Generator computes each Resource's ceiling from the declaration, and the `rsk::Shared::lock` API gives the data only inside a closure (crates/rsk/src/lib.rs).<br>Statements in: `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/history.rs`, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/sched.rs`.<br>23 source files cite a criterion of R8 in the matrix (2 of the files above among them). | `lemma_no_other_holder` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/sched.rs:472`): In a valid state with a Job on top that may access Resource r, any entry of the held-Resource stack for r belongs to that Job itself: no other Job holds r.<br>`lemma_deadlock_free` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/sched.rs:286`): In every valid state: the Job on top waits for no Resource; every pending Job that is not eligible either has a Job in progress or is blocked by some Job on the stack; and a blocker is in progress and is itself blocked by nothing. So no cycle of waiting exists.<br>`lemma_blocked_by_one_holder` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/sched.rs:1017`): A pending Task whose Priority is above the Job on top but not above the ceiling is kept out by a held Resource whose ceiling is at least its Priority and whose holder has a lower Priority.<br>`lemma_ceiling_restored` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/history.rs:652`): In any well-formed history, at the unlock that matches a lock (the held-Resource stack never shorter in between), the stack is what it was before the lock and the ceiling is the value it had just before the lock. | **Proven:** Verus (4) of the statements in column 3.<br>**Checked:** `api_misuse_is_rejected_by_the_type_system` (re-entry, an escaping reference, an undeclared Resource do not compile).<br>**Tested (host):** `r47_1` (Loom and Shuttle interleavings of the dispatch and lock model).<br>Allocation rows: P-01, P-02, P-03, P-05, P-06.<br>Evidence_Items naming a criterion of R8: `proof-kernel-verus` (pass). | **Yes.** For R8.1 to R8.5, which are the properties the requirement asks to be proven, the statements say what the requirement says, about the Kernel's scheduler state. A lock by the Job on top finds any existing holder entry of that Resource to be the Job's own (so it never waits); a pending Job that is not eligible is blocked by exactly the kind of holder R8.4 describes (a lower-Priority Job holding a Resource whose ceiling reaches it); a blocker itself waits for nothing, so there is no cycle; and between a lock and its matching unlock the stack of held Resources and the ceiling return to what they were. R8.6, R8.7 and R8.10 are the type system's and the Generator's, shown by compile-fail cases. What the statements do not carry is time: R8.8's bounds are measured, and the length of the one blocking interval is the Analyzer's term.<br>Closed since: 2026-10-22 and 23: restore across preemptions, single blocking and deadlock freedom moved from written arguments to lemmas over the history. | The realisation of the ceiling in BASEPRI is the entry code's (see R7). Δ_lock_in and Δ_lock_out are measured. R8.9 (Resources released when a Job is ended by the Health_Monitor) is part of the response's contract (see R14), not cited here. |
| **R9** Periodic release and timer dispatch (R9.1 to R9.10, Phase P1).<br>Each periodic Task is released at its offset plus a whole number of periods, computed from the offset and period alone so that it never drifts; a Release that falls due while the previous one is still pending is discarded and counted; a Job not finished by its deadline is reported; and at the end of the declared operating duration the system enters its safe state. | The Kernel keeps one timer slot per timed event and a nominal instant per periodic Task; the timer entry serves every slot that is due (`Kernel::timer_event`, `periodic_release`, `deadline_miss` in crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs; the instants in logic/time.rs). One hardware timer compare is armed for the earliest slot (crates/rsk-kernel/src/arch/cm4/entry.rs).<br>Statements in: `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs`, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/time.rs`, `proofs/aeneas/lean/Sched/Time.lean`.<br>31 source files cite a criterion of R9 in the matrix (2 of the files above among them). | `advance_periodic` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/time.rs:235`): For a periodic Task with a valid timing record: either the function returns the next nominal instant, which equals the configured nominal instant of Job k+1, is within the operating duration, and is now the Task's nominal instant with its Job count one higher; or it returns nothing, because that instant would be past the operating duration, and nothing changed. No other Task's instant or count, and none of the sporadic records, change.<br>`timer_event` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs:2536`): Outside the safe state, every periodic Task whose nominal instant is due at the entry's reading has its Release served by this entry, and every other periodic Task's slot, instant and absent Release are as they were; sporadic Releases that become due keep their MIT spacing; in the safe state nothing happens.<br>`advance_periodic_cases` (Lean, `proofs/aeneas/lean/Sched/Time.lean:529`): On the code as extracted from the compiled crate: the function either returns nothing and leaves the timing record as it was, or returns an instant equal to the Task's nominal instant plus its period, within the operating duration, and stores it as the new nominal instant.<br>`timer_event_reading` (Lean, `proofs/aeneas/lean/Sched/Time.lean:502`): On the extracted code: after a timer entry the Kernel's reading is the larger of the value it was given and its reading before, and every slot the entry served was armed with its instant at or before that reading. | **Proven:** Lean (2), Verus (2) of the statements in column 3.<br>**Tested (rig):** `hil-release-timing` (823,317 periodic Releases at their nominal instants over an hour, lag within J_rel).<br>**Assumed:** `ASM-19` (the timer's near-counter compare rule, revised from the board's behaviour).<br>Allocation rows: P-07, P-08, P-09.<br>Evidence_Items naming a criterion of R9: `proof-kernel-verus` (pass). | **Weaker.** R9.3 is proven as stated: the next nominal instant is the offset plus (k+1) periods, whatever else happened, or there is none within the operating duration. R9.1's 'released at the nominal instant' is proven in the sense that every periodic Task whose nominal instant is at or before the reading the timer entry is given has its Release served in that entry. Weaker: 'no later than J_rel after the instant' (R9.2) and 'within Δ_detect' (R9.6) are about real time between the instant and the entry, which is measured on the board, not proven; and the reading itself comes from hardware the proof models only as a number.<br>Closed since: 2026-11-02: one unanswered stimulus pulse in the first hour-long run (still open against the fault-injection task). 2026-11-05: the link from armed slots to the Releases the entry makes was a comment; it is now a postcondition of `timer_event`. 2026-11-16: on the code as extracted, a periodic Task's nominal instant is shown to move by exactly its period (Sched/Time.lean). | J_rel and Δ_detect are measured over an hour with a margin. The hardware timer's compare rule has a near-counter exception found by test (HW-12, ASM-19). R9.10 is the rig's hour-long run, on one Application. |
| **R10** Sporadic release and MIT enforcement (R10.1 to R10.9, Phase P1).<br>When an event arrives for a sporadic Task, the Kernel releases the Task only if no Release is waiting and at least one minimum inter-arrival time (MIT) has passed since the last one; otherwise it holds the event to the end of the MIT or drops it, records a violation, and applies the Partition's fault response once the violations pass a declared threshold. | The Kernel's intake function decides accept, defer or discard from the Task's last accepted instant and its MIT, counts the violation against the source's Partition, and masks the source for one MIT after every outcome (crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs, `Kernel::intake`; the timing record in logic/time.rs). The interrupt handler that calls it, and which Partition it names as the source, are in crates/rsk-kernel/src/arch/cm4/entry.rs and the generated tables.<br>Statements in: `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/history.rs`, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kani_harness.rs`, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs`, `proofs/aeneas/lean/Sched/Entry.lean`.<br>35 source files cite a criterion of R10 in the matrix (3 of the files above among them). | `intake` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs:2232`): Called on a valid Kernel state for a sporadic Task, the function leaves a valid state, only adds to the history, never lengthens the Job stack, and its result is one of the outcomes `intake_outcome` lists; the last accepted instants of all sporadic Tasks stay at least one MIT apart.<br>`intake_outcome` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs:2209`): The outcomes, by case. Not active (safe state, not started, Partition stopped, or too late to finish): nothing changes but the log and the source's mask. Active and acceptable: the Release is accepted. Active, not acceptable, no Release held, policy 'defer': the Release is deferred and a violation is applied. Otherwise (a Release already held, or policy 'discard'): nothing changes but the log and the mask, and a violation is applied.<br>`mit_accepts` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs:358`): An event is acceptable exactly when the Task holds no Release and either it has never been released or the present reading is at least one MIT after the last accepted instant.<br>`violation_applied` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs:497`): A violation adds one to the count of the Partition it is given. If the new count is within the Partition's threshold nothing else happens; if it is above, the Partition's declared fault response is applied.<br>`lemma_r10_4_count` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kernel.rs:221`): In a valid state, the Partition's counter plus one equals the number of violations recorded in the history since its last restart plus one, capped at the counter's maximum. So the counter is the count R10.4 means.<br>`lemma_mit_spacing_over_run` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/history.rs:589`): In any well-formed history, two Releases of the same sporadic Task have due instants at least one MIT apart.<br>`lemma_intake_count_bound` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/history.rs:574`): In any well-formed history, the intakes of one sporadic Task between two of its intake steps are spaced so that (their number minus one) times the MIT is less than the length of any window that holds both: at most one intake per MIT.<br>`intake_outcomes_match_r10` (Kani, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/kani_harness.rs:278`): On one small configuration, for every pair of event instants within its bounds and both policies, the compiled function accepts the first event, and treats a second one as R10.2 and R10.3 say. A bounded cross-check of the proof on the code as compiled.<br>`intake_decision_accept` (Lean, `proofs/aeneas/lean/Sched/Entry.lean:390`): On the code as extracted from the compiled crate: the decision function answers 'accept' only when its caller's flag says no Release is held and, if the Task was released before, the reading is at least one MIT after that instant. | **Proven:** Kani (1), Lean (1), Verus (7) of the statements in column 3.<br>**Tested (rig):** `hil-stress` (an hour-long interrupt storm: one intake per MIT window).<br>**Inspected:** `ASM-10` (the interrupt source's mask in hardware).<br>Allocation rows: P-08.<br>Evidence_Items naming a criterion of R10: `proof-kernel-verus` (pass). | **Weaker.** The statements cover R10.1 to R10.4 on the Kernel's state machine, with one difference in each direction. Weaker: time is the reading the Kernel takes when its handler runs, so a Release becomes due at that reading and not at 'the instant of the event' as R10.1 says; the two differ by the handler's latency, which is measured on the board and not proven. The Partition a violation is charged to is an argument of the function, so R10.7's choice of Partition is decided by the caller and the generated tables, not by these statements. Nothing cited here states R10.5 (Release_Signals), R10.6 (effective within J_rel) or R10.8 (messages kept in the Endpoint buffer). Narrower by decision: an event whose Job could not finish within the operating duration is not released; the requirement's note of 2026-11-13 says so.<br>Closed since: 2026-11-05: a discarded event left its interrupt source unmasked, so a source could fire again inside the MIT; every outcome now masks the source, and the count of intakes in any window is proven (`lemma_intake_count_bound`). | The handler's latency from the event to the reading (J_rel, Δ_stamp) is measured, not bounded statically. Attribution of a violation to the right Partition rests on the generated tables and inspection of the entry code. The hardware half of masking an interrupt source is by inspection (ASM-10). R10.5 and R10.8 have tests and no proof cited here. In the Lean run the MIT spacing is a condition of the run, not derived from the code, because the run's instants are not tied to the Kernel's readings. |
| **R11** FPU context management (R11.1 to R11.8, Phase P1).<br>A Job that uses floating point finds its floating-point registers exactly as it left them after any preemption, starts each Job with the declared control settings, and the cost and stack space of saving that state are accounted for. | The processor stacks half of the floating-point registers itself on every exception entry (the Kernel sets eager stacking at boot) and the dispatch stubs push and pop the other half in assembly (crates/rsk-kernel/src/arch/cm4/unsafe_module/stubs.rs). The control settings of a new Job come from Generated_Config through the default status register.<br>Statements in: .<br>10 source files cite a criterion of R11 in the matrix (0 of the files above among them). | None: no proof tool applies to this requirement, or none is cited. | **Tested (QEMU):** `test-qemu-spike-p1-demo` (the filter Task's state across 8 preempted Jobs).<br>**Tested (rig):** `hil-dt-hw-10` (register patterns across preemptions; the status register of a new context).<br>**Inspected:** `UJ-022` (the dispatch stub's save and restore of S16 to S31).<br>Allocation rows: P-11.<br>Evidence_Items naming a criterion of R11: `analysis-stack-p1-demo` (pass). | **No.** There is no formal statement of this requirement. Preservation is done by hardware stacking and assembly, which neither Verus nor Kani models; the evidence is tests: a floating-point Task whose state converges across preempted Jobs under QEMU and on the board, and the board's register-pattern probe across 141 preemptions. Since 2026-11-13 the stubs' instruction sequences are proven against a machine model, which covers the order of the pushes and pops but not the processor's own stacking.<br>Closed since: 2026-11-16: the rig's check of the status register a new floating-point context starts with compared against a record that read zero whether or not the probe had run (a declared non-zero initial value that was never in memory); the record now carries a written flag. | No proof tool applies to the hardware's stacking (testing evidence only, by decision). Δ_fp_save and Δ_fp_restore are measured at the method's resolution. One erratum's workaround (flush-to-zero) is a declaration option. |
| **R12** Boot-time configuration validation (R12.1 to R12.6, Phase P1).<br>Before the first Task is released the Kernel checks that the processor is the one the configuration was generated for and that its configuration tables are intact, and goes to the safe state if anything differs. | `boot_core` runs the hardware checks, the table validation (`Config::validate`, `Layout::validate`) and the checksums before it enables any interrupt (crates/rsk-kernel/src/arch/cm4/entry.rs; the validators in crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/mod.rs and mpu.rs).<br>Statements in: `crates/rsk-kernel/src/arch/cm4/entry.rs`, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/mod.rs`.<br>26 source files cite a criterion of R12 in the matrix (2 of the files above among them). | `validate` (Verus, `crates/rsk-logic/src/logic/mod.rs:239`): The function returns true exactly when the configuration is well-formed.<br>`boot_core` (Verus, `crates/rsk-kernel/src/arch/cm4/entry.rs:1082`): If boot reports success: the Kernel's invariant holds, the hardware model has every boot setting made, the entry code's own invariant holds with no Job in progress, the loaded MPU view matches the record, the vector tables are consistent, and every interrupt vector has its priority and its enable as the tables say. Nothing is stated for a boot that reports failure. | **Proven:** Verus (2) of the statements in column 3.<br>**Tested (rig):** `hil-boot-checks` (one mutated check per run, each ending in the safe state).<br>Allocation rows: P-14.<br>Evidence_Items naming a criterion of R12: `proof-kernel-verus` (pass). | **Weaker.** The table validation is proven exactly: the function returns true if and only if the configuration is well-formed, which is the property every other Kernel proof assumes. Boot's own contract says that if it succeeds the Kernel's invariant holds, the hardware model is in its booted state, and every vector has its priority and enable. The step from slots to message contents is the Kernel's copy, which is checked by Kani to stay in bounds and round-trip its words, and the model records only each message's first word.
